stories.headline: Lineups, live updates from Brewers-Rays World Series Game 5
stories.summary: After a dramatic Game 4, the Fall Classic continues tonight at Tropicana Field. Here's the latest.
stories.body:
After a dramatic comeback victory in Game 4, the Tampa Bay Rays lived to play another day.

The Rays won on a walk-off single by Ben Williamson in the 12th inning, denying the Milwaukee Brewers their first World Series title -- for now.

With Milwaukee up 3-1 in the series, will the Brewers raise the trophy on their second chance? Or will the Rays keep their postseason alive and push this series back to Milwaukee? And who is available to pitch for each team after Tuesday's marathon?

Stay tuned for pregame lineups, in-game action and postgame takeaways.

Key links: How to win World Series | Playoff MVP tracker | Full schedule

Milwaukee Brewers at Tampa Bay Rays (8 p.m. ET)
Starting pitchers: Jacob Misiorowski vs. TBD

What Brewers need to do to win: Play a clean game, something they've weirdly had a hard time doing in these playoffs. Brewers infielders have committed eight errors in the playoffs. Two of them occurred in Game 4 and led to runs, both of them errant throws from third base.

The Brewers should feel good about their chances in Game 5. They'll have their ace, Misiorowski, going up against a Rays team with few legitimate pitching options. And they'll be coming off a night in which their hitters produced 12 of the 13 hardest-hit balls with little to show for it. If they don't get in their own way, they'll be in good shape. -- Alden Gonzalez

What Rays must do to extend series: Make Misiorowski work. The Brewers have not relied on the hard-throwing right-hander for a heavy workload in the postseason. In Game 1, the presumptive NL Cy Young Award winner held the Rays to one run over five innings but was pulled after throwing just 78 pitches. He threw 88 pitches across four innings in his first playoff outing in the NLDS against the Padres and 94 pitches over 4⅓ innings in his NLCS start against the Dodgers. After using their best relievers heavily in Game 4, the Brewers could look for more length from Misiorowski in Game 5. They have the clear advantage in the pitching matchup, with Tampa Bay likely opting for a bullpen game. It's on Tampa Bay's lineup to erase the edge. -- Jorge Castillo

Who each team has available to pitch

In a nutshell, when you're a manager looking at the middle game of a three-game set and trying to map out your pitching plan for the finale, you don't want to see numbers like these from Game 4:

• Fifteen pitchers used over 23 innings and four hours, 20 minutes

• 367 pitches thrown

• 90 batters faced

If you're Tampa Bay skipper Kevin Cash, you'll take it. You won, so you get to play another one. The expenditure of pitching resources is a little harder to stomach for Milwaukee's Pat Murphy, whose team lost a late lead that could have closed out a championship.

"We drained a lot of pitching, as they did, and that's part of playing a tight ballgame," Murphy said.

Now that the dust has settled from a long, dramatic, season-extending contest, what's left? How does the pitching landscape look after this grinder of a Game 4?

Brewers

Murphy surprised no one after the game in saying that Misiorowski will start Game 5 on Wednesday. Misiorowski started Game 1 on Oct. 23, so he will be pitching on four days' rest. He made just four of his 30 starts this season on four days' rest but went 1-1 with a 1.64 ERA in those games. Over 22 innings, Misiorowski had 34 strikeouts and three walks in those games. Murphy would take those kind of numbers in Game 5.

Alas, Misiorowski hasn't pitched at that level during the postseason, and you have to figure that Murphy will once again need four or five innings from his bullpen. The big question will be how he might bridge the gap between Misiorowski and Trevor Megill or Aaron Ashby in a potential close-out situation.

Megill appeared in Game 4 but faced just one batter and threw five pitches to close out the eighth before giving way to Aaron Ashby. When asked at the podium after the game if he might have gotten more out of Megill, Murphy simply said, "Yes." He will likely need more in Game 5.

Ashby went 2⅓ innings but retired all seven batters he faced and threw just 31 pitches, a total he has surpassed 11 times this season. Ashby groused about being removed Tuesday, but since he didn't pitch in Game 3 and, after Game 5, there will either be a travel day or the season will be over, you have to figure Ashby can give Murphy at least an inning.

The same holds true for Abner Uribe, who threw two innings but faced the minimum of six batters, whom he retired on just 19 pitches. He also didn't pitch the Game 3 blowout, so he should be ready for an inning Wednesday.

Thus Murphy should have an ideal plan in place: Misiorowski to some progression of Uribe, Ashby and Megill. Whether he needs another reliever or relievers in addition to that will depend on the score and Misiorowski's effectiveness.

Rays

Things are trickier for the Rays even though they used one fewer pitcher than Milwaukee in Game 4. While their top relievers should be OK -- Bryan Baker, Kevin Kelly and Cam Booser all appeared but didn't have to labor through their outings -- the Rays probably can't roll out one of their primary starters and hope he goes deep.

After Game 4, Cash said that the Rays would be looking at their options and that no decision had been made. One obvious possibility would be to start Game 2 starter Drew Rasmussen on short rest. Rasmussen only went 3⅔ innings but threw 89 pitches to do it.

If Cash opts to start Rasmussen, it might be for a shorter outing, which would be less than ideal. If Cash can find an alternative to navigate the game while keeping Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta on normal rest, that would be ideal. The big problem there of course is that the Rays have to win Game 4 or that's that.

The monkey wrench in the Rays' plan was that Game 1 starter Nick Martinez came out of the bullpen in Game 4 and worked two innings, throwing 33 pitches. So the Rays' problems start at the outset. Cash will likely opt for some kind of bullpen game, perhaps with Rasmussen in a bulk role, but we'll see.

However the Rays plan it, they are just glad they have a game to plan for. -- Bradford Doolittle

stories.headline: What are the Warriors' options as Kristaps Porzingis remains away from the team?
stories.summary: Can the Warriors find a trade partner? Void Kristaps Porzingis' contract? Here's everything we know about the situation, and what could come next.
stories.body:
ON OPENING NIGHT of his 15th NBA season, Draymond Green -- generously listed at 6-foot-6 -- was slotted as the Golden State Warriors' starting center despite a continued organizational understanding about the accumulated toll it takes on his 36-year-old body.

The Warriors' staff gave Green a physical reprieve two nights later against the Memphis Grizzlies' jumbo front line. But circumstances, which include Al Horford's inability to play bigger minutes in his 20th season, forced Golden State to start Graham Ike, a two-way undrafted center out of Gonzaga in his second career game.

That still left Green out there in the late deciding moments attempting to box out the 7-4 Zach Edey. After failing to wall him off on a defensive rebound, Green committed a crucial frustration foul while the Warriors blew a 12-point lead and fell to 0-2 for the first time since 2020-21.

"We got what we got," Green said when asked about the eroded state of the Warriors' center position. "So we got to make it do what it do."

The Warriors feel part of the reason for their 37-45 failure a season ago was a woe-is-me attitude about the schedule and injury misfortune, team sources said, so they have taken a purposeful no-excuse approach this regular season.

That has meant an out-of-sight, out-of-mind strategy when it comes to the ongoing absence of presumed starting center Kristaps Porzingis, who was re-signed this summer despite missing 90 games over the past two seasons with three different teams. Ever since Porzingis called out of work one day prior to training camp, the front office instructed Steve Kerr to strategize and prep his team as if Porzingis was a nonfactor.

General manager Mike Dunleavy and lead medical decision maker Rick Celebrini are the only members of the team's staff who've been in communication with Porzingis during his absence. Kerr has bristled at nearly every Porzingis question in recent weeks.

"I don't know," Kerr said when asked for a recent update. "I don't really have anything else to add on this."

The decision to make a $20 million bet on the now-invisible Porzingis this offseason looms large over their 1-3 start and their murky path forward. On opening night, the same day ESPN reported the Warriors were beginning to explore possible trade routes while Porzingis contemplates his basketball future, opposing center Walker Kessler dunked on them 10 times, the most in a game for a Los Angeles Lakers center since Shaquille O'Neal in 2003.

In the aftermath, the always diplomatic Stephen Curry was asked about the unfortunate nature of Porzingis' indefinite absence and the impact it is having on his team.

"Aggggh," Curry said, tapping on the table as his frustration seeped through. "It's a hard one for all reasons."

Curry twice made sure to mention the human component, expressing sympathy for Porzingis, who has made public the lingering impact he said he still feels after contracting an upper respiratory viral illness while with the Boston Celtics two seasons ago.

"We always said availability was a big factor for our team with all the guys we have out," Curry said. "It's no secret that the [center] spot is an important one for us, especially with his skill set. It's hard to talk about without keeping the humanity of it in mind. But it is a tough one to figure out."

Team sources continue to express an extreme level of pessimism that Porzingis will ever play for the Warriors again, but he could end up helping the organization in another way, because his contract, which is only guaranteed for $3 million next season, could still prove to be valuable in executing a trade.

Here is everything we know as the situation remains in limbo.

How did Porzingis and the Warriors get here?
Porzingis' current salary slot was actually created during the summer of 2025, during one of the strangest restricted free agency standoffs in recent memory. Dunleavy and the Warriors were uneasy about committing long-term to Jonathan Kuminga, but felt he still held more value and upside than the sign-and-trade offers on the table.

So they stood firm in negotiations and eventually compromised with Kuminga on a two-year, $46.8 million deal that included a team option and a requirement that Kuminga waive his implicit no-trade clause. They were hopeful he'd contribute but made their motives clear enough during negotiations that Kuminga's side felt he was being turned into a human trade exception.

The Warriors flipped his contract to Atlanta for Porzingis' expiring $30.7 million contract in February, maintaining salary flexibility while believing they could manage Porzingis' health well enough to get some production out of him.

It worked decently. Porzingis appeared in 15 of the team's last 20 games and averaged 16.1 points, 5.3 rebounds and 1.1 blocks. That gave the front office and medical staff enough confidence to greenlight a two-year, $40 million extension in late June for a player who expressed a desire to continue his NBA career.

Still, the Warriors built in protections for a move they knew carried major risk by only guaranteeing $3 million of the $20 million in the second season. They also structured the extension so Porzingis could be traded immediately instead of having to wait until Dec. 15.

But Dunleavy and the Warriors held belief that Porzingis would be an available rotation piece for chunks of the schedule, not just a tradable contract. There was pre-camp buzz from the coaching staff about the intriguing nature of a Yaxel Lendeborg, Green, Porzingis front line.

Porzingis was in the practice facility getting court work the week prior to training camp and attended Jimmy Butler's player-led event in San Diego in late September. But optimism faded as team sources in attendance described Porzingis as indifferent and uninterested in participating in scrimmages and strenuous on-court prep work at the event -- a blaring signal of what was on the horizon.

What are the Warriors' options with Porzingis?
Porzingis called Dunleavy and stepped away from the team on the eve of training camp to deal with what they deemed a private health matter. The Warriors gave him some space initially but expected him to return to the facility and be around his teammates and the medical staff, team sources said.

After a meeting with Celebrini and Dunleavy in early October, the team sent out a statement declaring he would be around. It didn't last. Porzingis hasn't returned to the facility and the organization shifted his official status from out with "general illness" (as they'd listed during his absences last season) to "not with team," a purposeful change. This can no longer be described as an excused absence for the center.

Porzingis' unwillingness to be present at the Warriors' facility could be deemed a failure to render his services -- a reality that has been raised internally, sources said -- and could be used in an attempt to void his entire contract. But that would present its own complications, unless Porzingis expressed an intention to retire and willingly gave all the money back.

The Warriors are currently $20.4 million into the luxury tax. Wiping away Porzingis' salary erases nearly all of their tax bill, ducks them under the first apron and gives them more trade flexibility, but it doesn't free up a major roster-building tool. They'd only be able to add a player on the minimum via free agency.

The Warriors had a similar situation two seasons ago. They signed De'Anthony Melton to a one-year, $12.8 million deal in July 2024. He tore an ACL in early November and was ruled out for the season.

In response, Dunleavy lined up a trade with the Brooklyn Nets for Dennis Schroder, set to be executed on the first day Schroder was eligible to be traded (Dec. 15). It cost them a net of two second-round picks. Schroder played 24 games with the Warriors before he was traded as part of a deadline deal to acquire Butler.

That'd profile as a preferred route for the Warriors in this current Porzingis jam -- utilizing a minor asset to acquire a usable rotation player in the interim while maintaining the flexibility to repackage that expiring number for a larger swing at the deadline.

But under the new anti-tanking rules, there aren't any obvious trade partners ready to part with a usable player for a minor asset, especially in late October. Dunleavy has already gauged the temperature on the trade market, league sources said, but this is traditionally a quiet time in that respect. Front offices are typically in fact-gathering mode about their roster before making bigger-picture decisions closer to January and February.

Right now, the Warriors are showing a willingness to remain patient with the Porzingis contract and let the market materialize, league sources said. If Porzingis proves willing to give back a large chunk of money in a buyout, his expiring $20 million deal could become even more financially appealing for an eventual trade partner attempting to gain some financial benefit.

What is the Warriors' plan in the interim?
Lendeborg's immediate success has brightened the mood and eased some concern around the Warriors. The rookie wing had 31 points, 12 rebounds and six assists in a surprising blowout win in Denver on Monday night.

Lendeborg's power and size (6-foot-10, 241 pounds) has allowed them to downsize with Green at center while feeling bigger than their previous small-ball lineups. Lendeborg has 37 rebounds in four games.

Their current starting lineup (Lendeborg, Green, Curry, Brandin Podziemski and Gui Santos) is a plus-22 in a small early season sample. Horford -- limited to around 20 minutes per game and unable to play back-to-backs -- has looked fresh in brief doses.

While evolving through a semi-rebuild, the Warriors have shown an increased willingness to give opportunity to their youth in an effort to unearth some gems and improve their long-term outlook.

Ike has started two of the first four games, but will be limited to 50 games total unless the Warriors can convert his two-way contract to a full deal. Charles Bassey, the 25-year-old journeyman who is attempting to catch on with the Warriors after five previous stops, provides another big body off the bench.

"I love the attitude of this team," Kerr said. "I love the energy, the spirit. I like our talent. Then I think our two young big guys are good players."

stories.headline: Transfer rumors, news: Arsenal, Chelsea, City tracking PSG star Doué
stories.summary: Paris Saint-Germain winger Désiré Doué is being watched by three Premier League clubs and Bayern Munich. Transfer Talk has the latest.
stories.body:
Paris Saint-Germain winger Désiré Doué has caught the eye of some top Premier League clubs, while Juventus have made Monaco and USMNT striker Folarin Balogun their top priority for the January transfer window. Join us for the latest transfer news and rumors from around the globe.

Transfers home page | Men's summer grades | Women's grades

Trending rumors

- Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester City are monitoring Paris Saint-Germain winger Désiré Doué, alongside Bayern Munich, according to TEAMtalk. However, all the suitors face a setback in their hopes to sign him as PSG are progressing in talks over a contract extension with the 21-year-old France international to secure his future beyond 2029.

- Juventus have made Monaco striker Folarin Balogun their top priority for the January transfer window due to technical and financial factors, reports Tuttosport. The 25-year-old USMNT international is expected to leave Monaco after a €40 million summer move to Everton collapsed, while Atlético Madrid's Alexander Sørloth and Frosinone loanee Antonio Raimondo remain alternative targets for Juve.

- Chelsea have focused their attention on signing AFC Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott following their failed summer attempt, Florian Plettenberg reports. Liverpool are also looking to reunite Scott with Andoni Iraola, while TEAMtalk suggests the Cherries are targeting AZ Alkmaar's Kees Smit and Lazio's Kenneth Taylor as potential replacements for the 23-year-old England international.

- Chelsea, AC Milan, Galatasaray and Fenerbahçe are most keen on landing Brighton & Hove Albion midfielder Yasin Ayari, per TEAMtalk. Ayari, 23, has a deal that expires in the summer, though Brighton hold a one-year option to extend it which has created uncertainty around his future. The Sweden international has also been linked with Newcastle United, Arsenal, Manchester United, Liverpool, Atlético Madrid, Borussia Dortmund, Roma and Juventus.

- Former Manchester United winger Jadon Sancho has turned down an offer from Getafe after receiving a lucrative proposal from Saudi Arabia, according to Marca. The 26-year-old is a free agent and had requested a net salary of €3 million through the end of the season, which exceeded Getafe's financial capabilities.

OTHER RUMORS
- Chelsea remain admirers of Everton center back Jarrad Branthwaite, though the Toffees intend to keep him for the foreseeable future. (Football Insider)

- Chelsea, Manchester City, Arsenal, Tottenham Hotspur and Newcastle United all sent scouts to watch Club Brugge striker Nicolò Tresoldi score a hat-trick against Sint-Truiden. (TEAMtalk)

- Bayern Munich are monitoring Newcastle United loanee Nick Woltemade at Juventus as they evaluate a backup for Harry Kane. (Gazzetta dello Sport)

- Barcelona, Napoli, and Juventus are tracking Tottenham Hotspur midfielder Lucas Bergvall amid his limited first-team minutes this season. (TEAMtalk)

- Manchester United have shifted their January transfer priorities toward reinforcing their defensive unit. (Football Insider)

- Brighton & Hove Albion and RB Leipzig could make a January bid to sign Juventus winger Adin Licina, who is currently impressing on loan at Cremonese. (Tuttosport)

- Lecce are preparing for defender Tiago Gabriel to depart in January amidst growing interest from Everton. (Football Insider)

- Leeds United are targeting a cut-price January deal to sign Porto left back Zaidu Sanusi. (Football Insider)

- Right-back João Mário could seek a January exit from Fiorentina to secure greater playing time. (Nicolò Schira)

stories.headline: NHL Tonight: Previewing Devils-Avalanche, Wednesday's three other games
stories.summary: Find game previews, betting intel and broadcast information, along with stats and highlights here.
stories.body:
It's a lighter schedule of games for NHL fans Wednesday, but all four matchups are captivating for one reason or another.

That includes the next matchup in the Battle of Alberta, along with a rematch between the Avalanche and Devils after New Jersey's 4-3 win on Oct. 20.

Here's a look at what you need to know for each game, including betting info and broadcast details:

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

Philadelphia Flyers at Washington Capitals

7:30 p.m. ET (TNT) | WSH -238, O/U: 6.5

In the final season of Alex Ovechkin's record-breaking NHL career, he gets to play against all of his Metro Division rivals four times each. This will be the first showdown against the Flyers.

Ovechkin has 54 goals and 32 assists in 82 career regular-season games against Philly, including two tallies in the most recent matchup on March 31.

The two teams split their season series in 2025-26, and the Flyers would appear to need the two points quite a bit more given their lackluster start.

Calgary Flames at Edmonton Oilers

8:30 p.m. ET (ESPN) | EDM -218, O/U: 6.5

No matter the players involved, there is always a little extra juice when the NHL's two Alberta-based teams square off. That's no different this season, despite the fact that the Flames haven't made the postseason since 2022 -- when the Oilers knocked them out in five games in the second round.

This will be the first matchup between the clubs this season, and it will (likely) feature the NHL's second star of the week, Devin Cooley, in goal for the Flames.

On the other side, the Oilers have the NHL's first star of the week, Leon Draisaitl, who hopes to get the upper hand in this matchup. He'll have help; while Drasaitl is second in the NHL in scoring this season (24 points through 12 games), teammate Connor McDavid is first with 34 points.

New Jersey Devils at Colorado Avalanche

9 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | COL -192, O/U: 6.5

Just 25 hours after opening puck drop against the Central Division powerhouse Dallas Stars, the Devils will face off against the Central Division powerhouse Colorado Avalanche.

In the teams' first matchup this season, the Devils got out to a 3-1 lead early in the third period, and Jesper Boqvist put a puck into the empty net at 16:05. The Avs got two back -- both credited to Artturi Lehkonen -- but couldn't find the equalizer.

Will Wednesday's game include as exciting of a finish?

Toronto Maple Leafs at Seattle Kraken

10 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | TOR -115, O/U: 6.5

It's still quite early in the season, but both of these teams enter this contest in playoff positions in their respective divisions after missing out on the postseason fun in 2026.

The Leafs will hope they get an effort like the one they had Saturday in Edmonton (a 7-2 win) as opposed to Monday in Calgary (a 5-2 loss). Seattle has also had some inconsistent results as of late, with wins over the Mammoth and Red Wings sandwiched between blowout losses to the Panthers and Wild.

stories.headline: 'They smoke us': Why a moon astronaut thinks F1 is ahead of NASA
stories.summary:
150-char blurb
Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman explains why F1's engineering is ahead of NASA's, his admiration for Mercedes and what he learned on the moon.
stories.body:
Somewhere between Earth and the moon, Reid Wiseman encountered a problem. The windows of his Artemis II spacecraft were filthy.

It wasn't a mechanical failure, the haunting bleep of a master alarm or some other unforeseen consequence borne out of attempting to travel further than any human beings in history. Instead, the four astronauts aboard NASA's Artemis II mission had spent so much time with their faces pressed against the glass, gazing in awe at both the diminishing Earth in one direction and the extraordinary lunar landscape growing bigger in the other, that the windows were covered in smudges.

"We were looking out at Earth and we were looking out at the moon all the time," Wiseman told ESPN. "Victor [Glover], my pilot, made a comment when we got into our first orbit of Earth, he's like, 'that's the last time Reid ever looked inside [the spacecraft].'

- Nate Saunders on the contradictions of Austin's COTA

- How Kimi Antonelli can win the title in Mexico City

- Fernando Alonso slams 'low quality bottom third of the grid'

"We had to do a photo analysis of the windows so that the geology team could make sure there was no damage, or if they were seeing blemishes on lunar photography, they could relay it back. And I was looking at the windows before I got the camera out to do the survey, and I called down to Mission Control and said, 'hey, first, I need to clean them, because the amount of grease marks from our noses and foreheads on the windows, it was just completely covered.'"

For the commander of the first crewed mission to the moon in more than half a century, it was an understandable distraction. The view was unlike anything he had experienced before, even during his previous six-month stint aboard the International Space Station.

"We're human. Making sure the spacecraft is operating is of the prime of importance. But right underneath that is absorbing the experience. The thing that struck me most looking at the Earth is it got very small, and then it got, like, that big," Wiseman said, pushing his thumb and index finger almost completely together.

"But really looking at the moon was the three-dimensionality of everything. You're not looking through an atmosphere. Everything is crystal clear, everything. The blacks, the craters, the bumps, the sun hitting the crater rim, it was profoundly crystal clear, and all four of us felt that exact same thing. Your brain was having trouble processing the clarity with which we were seeing this three-dimensional moon right there out of the window."

Spine-tingling stuff, even if here it was slightly off-topic, at least in an official capacity.

The premise of Wiseman's interview time with ESPN was not primarily about space. Although when you're talking to someone who has travelled a quarter of a million miles from Earth, how could it be about anything else?

Sitting at Austin's Circuit of the Americas, Wiseman was not wearing the orange spacesuit of Artemis II, nor the familiar dark blue of NASA, but the white of Mercedes' Formula 1 team's team kit. Six months after returning from his historic journey around the moon, Wiseman became an ambassador for the German manufacturer. Last year, he and his daughter had attended the United States Grand Prix on general admission tickets. Then, for all intents and purposes, Wiseman was just another person baking in the Texas sun with thousands of other people. Returning a year later he can boast that he's one of just nine living humans to have seen the far side of the moon with their own eyes.

The setting of the interview prompted an obvious question.

How does NASA compare to Formula 1? The answer was surprising.

"Oh, they crush us," he replied. "I mean, the level of engineering here, they smoke us."

Wiseman's view is rooted in the priorities of the two disciplines. NASA places a premium on proven technology and backup systems, even if that means carrying additional weight into space to ensure the mission objectives are met. Formula 1, meanwhile, is about the relentless pursuit of performance and pushing the boundaries of engineering in search of even the smallest advantage. As we spoke, we were surrounded by Mercedes' race operation -- engineers, mechanics, media team, performance coaches, who have impressed him as much as the technology.

"In spaceflight, what we really need is tried and true, redundancy, and we can accept a little bit of a mass penalty," he said. "Here, they're just pushing everything to the next level, and just every single thing is ... it's not just the cars, it's the humans. You know, everybody's walking around with WHOOP straps, and monitoring everything about themselves. They're all basically athletes. They're all going all in at all times. I love the way they deal with human performance and mechanical performance."

The competition aspect of Formula 1 -- which pits Mercedes against 10 other teams every race -- is always going to skew a comparison between Antonelli's world and Wiseman's world. For the Artemis II commander, it's the hunger to win that sets Formula 1 apart.

"At the end of the day in our work, there's a really large team of experts that sit just under the fanfare, but are the ones that are the true heroes that have the real courage. And then on top are these people who are willing to push the envelope a little bit and go.

"What is a little different for us is I have a crew of four people that are together in the spacecraft and working to try to make this mission the best it can be. In these cars, it is George [Russell] going all in, killer instinct ... Kimi [Antonelli] going all in, killer instinct. Occasionally they might meet in a corner and then I'm like, 'oh dear god, let's get through the corner.'"

For Mercedes, that focus on performance has seen the German team climb back to the pinnacle of the sport this year. Wiseman was speaking ahead of a U.S. Grand Prix which saw Kimi Antonelli move to the verge of becoming the sport's youngest-ever world champion at 20 years old.

This weekend, he will almost certainly wrap it up in Mexico City.

Wiseman can remember his interaction with Antonelli in 2024, before he had even started racing in Formula 1. Even then, Wiseman could see traits that have helped propel Antonelli to the brink of history.

"I met Kimi briefly when he was touring the Johnson Space Centre, and he invited me to a race when he was there," Wiseman said.

"[He was] 17. When I met him, the first thing I thought was how astonishingly humble and down to earth he was. But at the same time, he's a little goofy, which I love, but he's just curious about everything. We were touring with a few other drivers, but Kimi was asking every question about every single thing, whether he needed the information or not. Those are the people I try to latch on to because that curiosity is so powerful.

"You walk around, why is that cloud there? Why is that bird flying? How is it doing that? Why are these tyres better than these tyres?"

Antonelli's rise came after a rollercoaster rookie season in 2025. The young Italian has this year made a lot of the support network Mercedes put around him - team boss Toto Wolff's arm-over-the-shoulder approach to some of Antonelli's early mistakes were key. So has been the oversight of his race engineer, Peter Bonnington, who brought with him the experience of working in the same role with Lewis Hamilton.

Even here, Wiseman cannot help but point to where the two worlds overlap in some way.

"I chuckle at the way Bono and Kimi talk [on the radio]. It feels exactly like us in space, where we'll say something to the engineering team, and then when we unkey the mic, the engineering team will be like, 'they don't know what they're talking about', and then they'll come up with an answer for us, and they'll send it back. I love hearing that.

"I love it when the engineers and the drivers joke around on the radio, and you can just tell. It's just a great relationship."

Wiseman's link-up with Mercedes is a unique thing, but he feels right at home. He admits he was never one of those "crazy space kids" who could name every Apollo astronaut or had Neil Armstrong as a boyhood hero. But there was an interest in racing from a young age. He grew up going to NASCAR races with his father in Delaware, although they never did fulfill their dream of watching an Indy 500 together. His first chance to see Formula 1 in person was in 2023, invited by McLaren and Mercedes.

Wiseman admits he initially wondered what to expect from the "terrifying Toto Wolff," but has since come to admire the culture the Mercedes boss has established.

"What really struck me was, he's actually not scary, he's hilarious in his own humour. What I noticed as we were here, if you look around this place, there's no flash, it's just professionalism. 'We were going to go get the job done, and not just on the track.' It's the way they take care of the fans, the way they take care of the sponsors, the way they take care of the engineering team."

As he continued, Wiseman gestured over to Mercedes reserve driver Fred Vesti for another anecdote. "I went out for a run this morning with the engineers and did a swim down in Austin with them, and then I couldn't keep up on the way home, so I ran with Fred Vesti. He hung back and ran with me. The culture here always comes from the top. You can just tell Toto has one hell of a racing team that also knows how to take care of people."

Here is where he thinks NASA can learn a great deal from Formula 1's super-active team members. "Astronauts have to put a pretty good premium on our own health and physical conditioning, because we're going to be weightless, and our bones and our muscles are going to waste during the mission.

"So we put a big premium on that. We don't put as big of a premium on our support team and making sure they are at their highest level, and I think we can raise their level of expertise. They spend a lot of their days sitting in chairs, analysing data, and most of them would probably be upset if I said, let's go run three miles, but I think we can elevate the human performance, and we should really look at that. Because you look around in this team, everybody is fit, they're hungry, they're getting after it, and I think we can elevate the team [at NASA]."

Wiseman was brought to Mercedes to tell these kinds of stories. His role is to work with team partners, sponsors and guests to explain the overlap between the two worlds and, of course, to tell captivating stories about his own experiences. It's easy to see what he brings to the table. Had our interview not already overrun its 15-minute slot, it would have been easy to have kept going and going. "Toto likes the way I communicate," he said. "I think [guests] also like hearing stories of four humans that have gone further from Earth than anyone else. And I think there's just a lot of good storytelling and a sense of adventure that comes from that."

Inevitably, of course, our conversation drifted back to space.

Wiseman's anecdotes do not end with the stories he can tell verbally. At one point, he reached for his phone to show a picture with legendary Apollo-era flight director Gene Kranz, now 91, and Apollo 13 astronaut Fred Haise, taken earlier that week. Scattered through his camera roll were photographs he had taken himself of the moon from inside the spacecraft, through those smudged windows. Not a bad collection of snaps to have at your fingertips.

The Artemis II mission captivated a worldwide audience. In one of its most poignant moments, Wiseman's crewmates surprised him by naming a lunar crater in honour of his late wife, Carroll. But while millions of people followed their every move from Earth, the four astronauts were experiencing something rather different.

It is only since returning home that Wiseman has begun to appreciate just how much the mission meant to those watching.

"One thing that has been so rewarding is fame is not really that fun. I don't know how Kimi and George deal with that," he said. "But I was at an airport over in Europe the other day, and a dad came over to me and said, 'Hey, my daughter thinks you're Reid Wiseman. Are you?' And I said, yes, I am.

"And he turns to her, and this 10-year-old girl from the Philippines comes running over and just gave me the biggest hug. She knew everything about Christina, everything about Victor, everything about Jeremy.

"And I took this little medallion off my backpack and gave it to her, and she was so emotional. That stuff just is, it's all we could have ever wished for."

It was one of countless stories Wiseman and his crewmates have been hearing since they returned, providing a new perspective on a journey they are still coming to terms with themselves.

"We were all together three weeks ago. And we hadn't been together in a few weeks, and we were like, how's everything going? What are you feeling right now?

"And we all have this common feeling of we're starting to understand that we experienced this mission, but Earth experienced it. And now we're loving hearing the stories.

"Now that we've kind of processed the mission, we're listening to the stories from our friends at launch, when Carroll Crater was named, the amount of emotion that was involved in that. People were waking up and turning on the YouTube channel to see where are they today, what's going on.

"And we realised we went on a mission, but actually Earth kind of did too."

stories.headline: Salkilld, Saint Denis to headline UFC Fight Night in Sydney
stories.summary: West Australian Quillan Salkilld will headline a UFC Fight Night lightweight matchup with Benoît Saint Denis in Sydney in February.
stories.body:
West Australian Quillan Salkilld will return to the Octagon in Sydney, after it was confirmed he'll headline the UFC Fight Night with a lightweight bout against Frenchman Benoît Saint Denis on February 7 (AEDT).

Salkilld, 26, is a former Australian rules footballer who turned to MMA after leaving school at 16, and boasts an impressive 13-1 professional record (6-0 in UFC) with five 'performance of the night' bonuses.

The Broome native has won four consecutive fights with a first-round finish, most recently submitting Mateusz Gamrot in their UFC Fight Night clash in Perth in August. He's widely regarded as Australia's next big combat star.

Meanwhile Saint Denis, 30, is one of the lightweight division's most dangerous finishers, and has a 17-4 professional record.

Peter Kloczko, senior vice president of UFC Australia and New Zealand, said the Fight Night -- to take place at Sydney's Afterpay Arena -- would be an "unforgettable event" featuring one of Australia's brightest young stars.

"UFC Fight Night Sydney is set to be another huge moment for Australian fans, and Quillan Salkilld versus Benoît Saint Denis is a main event that delivers everything we look for in this sport," he said in the official release.

"Quillan has been one of the breakout stars of the UFC's lightweight division, while Benoît is one of the most dangerous and exciting finishers in the sport. Bringing this fight to Sydney will make for an unforgettable night."

Further fights on the card will be released in due course.

stories.headline: Power to burn and a 'trademark' goal: why Ethan Drever has rocketed up draft boards
stories.summary: Growing up an Essendon supporter, Ethan Drever hasn't 'seen anything' like success. But his rise up draft boards could have him in the frame to be his childhood club's first pick, writes Jasper Chellappah.
stories.body:
Ethan Drever had absolutely no choice on his AFL team. As a newborn he was put in an Essendon jumper at the hospital and he's been a Bomber ever since.

It's been a rough 18 years of fandom since, and he's got some thoughts about his dad's decision.

"I'm [born in] 2008, I haven't seen anything!" he tells ESPN with a grin - and a grimace.

"Dad tells me about his success and I'm like, 'You don't have to rub it in like that.'"

The Dons are entering a new era in 2027 under Mark McVeigh and it's being driven through the draft. They snagged Sullivan Robey, Jacob Farrow, and Dyson Sharp in the first round 12 months ago and now own pick 1 in the upcoming draft.

Drever also has a lot of thoughts about those drafted before him.

"They've got some good young boys in there now. Robey, Sharp, they're gonna be so good.

"I like Farrow. He should be kicking in and doing all that, he needs to be in priority positions. That's what he's gonna be doing in the future.

"Just that halfback, I reckon he's gonna be really good... he's a beautiful left foot kick."

After a dour two-win season the Bombers have first call on Drever, with the 188cm on-baller strongly linked at the top of the board.

He's an electric runner with the intent to tackle, chase, and pressure - something that hasn't been a trait of Essendon's list for a long time.

Asked what he thinks when watching his boyhood club each weekend, Drever's response would prick the ears of all Bombers fans.

"It'd be nice to be out there and sort of help the boys out, that's kinda what I'm thinking!"

The Vic Country MVP and Rebels best and fairest produced a remarkable season. His star has risen from a first-round chance to the very top of the open pool.

He may have the most translatable traits to AFL level of any prospect. Drever is an elite power athlete, recording a 2.92 second 20 metre sprint which comes across in the tape. He bursts out of the contest with driving legs and loves to exit forward of the stoppage to inflict maximum damage.

His ultra consistent season has come about without any injury concerns, something all other top prospects this year haven't been able to say.

"It's been good not to have to sit on the sidelines this year at all and I can just keep playing consistent footy," he says.

"I only missed one [game] which was just after champs, I just had a break."

Drever lays claim to a pretty handy trademark. On six separate occasions this season he's collected the ball -- either out of a stoppage or in open play -- and powered away from opponents into the forward half of the ground.

From there his long running gait and elite top speed helps him separate from chasing defenders and break the paint of 50 to drive home sensational goals.

"I have heard it's called the trademark goal now. I don't know where that's really come from, it's just a natural thing I guess. I just like to run and have a ping from outside 50," Drever tells ESPN.

"Definitely one of my traits is just my power, especially this year. Building up over the pre-season and definitely my two-way running.

"It's the long-term goal to move into the midfield and be a bit of a Jordan Dawson with his two-way running. I love Finn Callaghan, how he plays. Those two are really great role models for me.

"I think Hugh McCluggage as well, I've watched him a lot. I had a meeting with him this year, he's that sort of two-way runner as well and he's been really good for me."

Drever played 13 games for the Rebels this year in amongst commitments with the AFL Academy and Vic Country. He collected the ball 28 times to go with a goal a game, but he's not satisfied with just being an offensive weapon.

The Ballarat local is a tenacious presence in contests with the appetite to chase and tackle, racking up 6.5 per outing to frank his status as the best pure midfielder in the open pool.

At the draft combine he showed off a much-improved engine running a 6:27 minute 2km after going 20 seconds slower in the lead-up. It's a time that will put him towards the front of the pack on day one of pre-season.

Drever knows exactly what's required to be a midfielder at the next level, and he's determined to get there as soon as possible.

"My endurance side was a big goal of mine, obviously at the top level you've just got to be able to run all day.

"Honing in on my fundamentals and trying to get them the best I can as well. That's what the most important thing is because it's the little one percenters that make a difference in the AFL.

Drever is now on the precipice of living out his dream of becoming an AFL player, and it could be for his boyhood club as the top choice in the open pool of the draft.

That won't matter to him, so long as he gets his opportunity to shine on the big stage.

"I don't really care [if I go at pick 1]. It's nice to have my name up in consideration alongside those boys but I'll just be happy to be picked up wherever I go."

stories.headline: Lens fans banned from Liverpool match for throwing flares vs. Brugge
stories.summary: Fans of Ligue 1 club Lens were banned from buying tickets for a Champions League game at Liverpool by a UEFA disciplinary ruling Tuesday.
stories.body:
NYON, Switzerland -- Fans of Ligue 1 club Lens were banned from buying tickets for a Champions League game at Liverpool by a UEFA disciplinary ruling on Tuesday.

Lens fans lit dozens of flares and threw some toward rival supporters and the field, forcing the team's Champions League game at Club Brugge last week to be stopped briefly. Lens lost 3-0.

The club already were on probation by UEFA for fans lighting flares and fireworks at a previous Champions League game at Slavia Prague in September.

UEFA said its appeals judges imposed a ban on Lens selling tickets to fans for two Champions League away games.

The sanction will be served when Lens play at Leipzig on Nov. 24 and at Liverpool at Anfield on Jan. 27. A third game ban is deferred for a two-year probationary period.

UEFA said Lens were fined €80,000 ($89,000) for charges of "lighting and throwing of pyrotechnics as well as for acts of damage."

stories.headline: Bafana boss Pitso Mosimane's latest South Africa squad shows favouritism fears were unfounded
stories.summary: Mosimane has made several changes from his first preliminary squad, which he announced almost immediately after taking charge at the beginning of September.
stories.body:
When Pitso Mosimane returned as Bafana Bafana head coach, sceptics feared that his proximity to South African club football would lead to an erosion of the meritocratic culture Hugo Broos had built, but the 62-year-old's second preliminary squad suggests it has only been enhanced.

Mosimane began his tenure with Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifying wins over Guinea and Eritrea and a friendly victory over Egypt. Next up is the AFCON qualifying double-header against Kenya on Nov. 13 & 17.

Mosimane has made several changes from his first preliminary squad, which he announced almost immediately after taking charge at the beginning of September.

Chicago Fire's Mbekezeli Mbokazi has returned from injury, while Aden McCarthy, Botiumelo Radiopane, Nqaba Xulu, Luke le Roux, Thalente Mbatha, Nkosikhona Radebe, Devin Titus and Thakasani Mbanjwa have also received call-ups.

For every one of these call-ups, a layman can deduce a clear possible motive. McCarthy is the most obvious among them -- he has consistently featured at centre-back for Sabah in the UEFA Champions League and performed well at the highest level.

Radiopane and Xulu are in hot scoring form domestically for Orlando Pirates and Richards Bay respectively. Titus has earned his place with a strong start to life at MAS Fes in Morocco. Mbatha is back from injury and le Roux on the books of a new club at Cercle Brugge after struggling for game time at Portsmouth.

Radebe adds a right-back option from an in-form AmaZulu side with Mamelodi Sundowns' Khuliso Mudau still on the mend from injury. Mbanjwa is rewarded for a strong start to the season in goal for Golden Arrows.

Yanela Mbuthuma and Shandre Campbell -- both of whom have experienced dips in form and fortune at club level since the last international break -- are notable absentees.

In cutting two players he had given opportunities to after they had been mostly overlooked by Broos, Mosimane suggested he is willing to operate without fear or favour.

When 'Jingles' was on the verge of being appointed, Broos was quoted as telling Het Nieuwsblad: "You know, South Africa still don't have a coach. The candidate is Pitso Mosimane, a successful South African coach.

"But they know that if he comes in, they'll go five years back in time. Club owners and agents calling coaches to influence the squad selection. I threw all of them out. If one called, I would say bluntly: 'I don't talk with agents'."

The concern over agents and owners trying their luck in influencing the Bafana head coach may have been well-founded. Broos was not the first to complain of this within the national team setup.

However, questioning if Mosimane himself was open to influence without proof he was willing to make publicly available was ill-advised. It is impossible to accurately speculate on what conversations have or have not gone on between Mosimane and club owners and agents in the two months since then, but what is clear is that his team selection has been thoroughly meritocratic.

The momentum he has garnered is reminiscent of what Broos achieved in the first six months of his tenure.

At the time, the Belgian's irreverent team selection and approach to squad culture put everybody on their toes and led to an uptick in results. After they had failed to qualify for AFCON 2021 immediately before Broos was appointed, the Belgian fell narrowly short of steering Bafana into qualification playoffs for the 2022 World Cup.

In subsequent years, he kicked on and led Bafana to third place at AFCON 2023 (held belatedly in Ivory Coast in early 2024) and the 2026 World Cup round of 32.

When discussing the most successful Bafana Bafana coaches of all-time, Broos should be placed alongside Clive Barker in the top two. However, even the brightest tacticians eventually settle on patterns in their squad selection, and towards the end of his tenure, the Belgian became more predictable in certain aspects.

There was a fairly settled back five of Ronwen Williams, Aubrey Modiba, Mbokazi, Ime Okon and Mudau, and until he switched up his attacking plan to revive the FIFA World Cup campaign, Broos was likely to start Lyle Foster upfront with Evidence Makgopa the main alternative.

In midfield, Teboho Mokoena was a near certain starter and Sphephelo Sithole the clear preferred option alongside him, although Broos occasionally tinkered with his formation and left room for the likes of Bathusi Aubaas and the late Jayden Adams in the holding role. Nkosinathi Sibisi was considered another option, occasionally stepping out from the back into midfield.

Mosimane's arrival has reopened competition for places in these positions. Brooklyn Poggenpoel is retained in the squad after impressing in midfield over the last international break.

After Mbuthuma's minutes upfront, Radiopane and Xulu have been given a chance to earn theirs. Foster has made a second successive preliminary squad, although he failed to make the final squad last time out while in the process of leaving Burnley on loan to Houston Dynamo and settling in.

Fawaaz Basadien, Olwethu Makhanya, and McCarthy are in consideration in the backline. Mudau is, however, still the likely first-choice at right-back for the time being when he returns to full fitness. Still, Mosimane has done well to identify alternatives.

Mosimane declined to get drawn into a war of words with Broos over anything not directly related to matters on the pitch and instead praised his predecessor's impressive record as Bafana head coach.

In his first stint, Mosimane may not have succeeded in the hotseat. However, early results and his approach to team selection suggest he has justified the decision of the South African Football Association (SAFA) to give him a second chance and trust him to navigate the role without fear or favour to anyone.

DEF: Aubrey Modiba, Samukele Kabini, Fawaaz Basadien, Nkosikhona Radebe, Thapelo Morena, Thabang Matuludi, Olwethu Makhanya, Khulumani Ndamane, Ime Okon, Lebone Seema, Nkosinathi Sibisi, Mbekezeli Mbokazi, Aden McCarthy
